issues.legal_issue: An appellate court may consider later developments that are genuine, relevant, and important to deciding the dispute or preventing injustice.
material_facts: In the appeals, competent authorities and courts had made findings that the claimant was not the asserted adopted heir and that the adoption document was forged or fabricated.
The findings went to the basis of the claimant’s asserted rights in the land, and the claimant did not effectively deny the existence of the orders recording them.
issues.conclusion: The later developments could and should be considered at the appellate stage, and they were sufficient to disentitle the claimant from relief and to dismiss the appeals.
issues.legal_principle: Relevant and genuine subsequent facts may be considered at the appellate stage when necessary to decide the issues effectively, achieve substantial justice, or prevent a miscarriage of justice. The Court relied on competent judicial and statutory authorities’ orders concerning the asserted adoption and entitlement; it cited no earlier case for this principle.

predicates.appeal_proceeding: A party appealed a decision concerning its claimed rights in property.
predicates.later_authoritative_findings_undermine_c: Competent adjudicative bodies later made findings that undermine the factual basis of the appealing party’s claimed entitlement.
predicates.findings_not_effectively_denied: The appealing party did not effectively deny the existence of the later findings or orders.

issues.definition: When a party appeals a property decision and later authoritative findings undermine its claimed entitlement without being effectively denied, the appellate court may consider those developments and deny relief.

issues.legal_issue: A surrender of tenancy rights completed before statutory prior-sanction requirements took effect was not invalid merely for lacking that sanction or for occurring before the end of the agricultural year.
material_facts: The tenancy was surrendered by registered deed in 1942.
The statutory requirement for prior sanction before the relevant transfer was introduced later and took effect in 1948.
The surrender occurred before the end of the agricultural year.
issues.conclusion: The surrender was not invalid for want of prior sanction or because it was made before the end of the agricultural year, and the High Court’s reasoning on those points required no interference.
issues.legal_principle: The validity of the surrender is governed by the Chotanagpur Tenancy Act as it stood when the surrender occurred. Sections 46 and 72, as then in force, did not require prior permission of the Deputy Commissioner for the surrender at issue, and the later amendment to Section 46 took effect in 1948. The Court distinguished Pandey Oraon v. Ram Chandra Sahu, (1992) Supp. (2) SCC 77, and Brisa Munda v. Chando Kumari, (1996) 9 SCC 545, because they did not decide the law applicable to a surrender completed before the 1947 amendment took effect.

predicates.tenancy_surrender_proceeding: The dispute concerns the validity of a surrender of tenancy rights.
predicates.surrender_preceded_prior_sanction_requir: The tenant completed the surrender before a statutory requirement for prior official sanction applied to that surrender.
predicates.surrender_occurred_before_agricultural_y: The tenant completed the surrender before the agricultural year ended.

issues.definition: A tenancy surrender completed before a prior-sanction requirement applied is not invalid merely because it lacked that later-required sanction or occurred before the agricultural year ended.

issues.legal_issue: The phrase indicating that a restoration power may be exercised at any time does not make the power unlimited in time or disregard rights acquired in the meantime.
material_facts: Proceedings under the restoration provision were initiated many years after the surrender and after other persons had acquired rights under ordinary law.
The character of the land and the nature of the interest surrendered, which could affect the provision’s applicability, remained disputed.
issues.conclusion: The restoration power could not be treated as exercisable without any time limit and without regard to intervening rights; the Court considered it inappropriate to accept the contrary contention in these proceedings.
issues.legal_principle: The words “if at any time” in Section 71A of the Chotanagpur Tenancy Act do not, by themselves, authorize exercise of the power without a time limit and without regard to rights acquired under ordinary law and the Law of Limitation in the meantime. The Court discussed Pandey Oraon v. Ram Chandra Sahu, (1992) Supp. (2) SCC 77, and Brisa Munda v. Chando Kumari, (1996) 9 SCC 545, but held that neither decided the applicability of Section 71A to a surrender completed before the later amendments.

predicates.restoration_proceeding: A proceeding seeks restoration of land under a statutory restoration power.
predicates.long_delay_since_transfer: The restoration proceeding began many years after the relevant transfer or surrender.
predicates.intervening_rights_acquired: Other persons acquired rights in the land under ordinary law during the interval.

issues.definition: In a restoration proceeding brought after a long delay during which others acquired rights, the statutory power is not timeless or indifferent to those intervening rights.

issues.legal_issue: A non-tribal holder’s status alone does not establish that land must be allotted to another tribal person when the statutory character of the land and the interest transferred remain unresolved.
material_facts: The appellant argued that the non-tribal respondents could not retain the land and that it had to be allotted to a tribal person.
The High Court had left unresolved whether the land was of a character, or the surrendered interest was of a kind, that brought the property within the relevant statutory provisions.
The restoration proceedings had been pursued after a substantial delay and intervening rights had arisen.
issues.conclusion: The Court rejected the contention that the non-tribal respondents had to be displaced and the land allotted to another tribal person in these proceedings.
issues.legal_principle: The applicability of the statutory provisions depended in part on the character of the land and the nature of the interest surrendered. Non-tribal ownership alone did not establish that the land had to be allotted to another tribal person, particularly where those matters remained unresolved and the claim was advanced after a substantial delay. The Court considered the scope of Section 71A of the Chotanagpur Tenancy Act and its reasoning concerning the timing of restoration proceedings.

predicates.restoration_proceeding: A proceeding seeks restoration or reallocation of land under a statutory power.
predicates.holder_is_non_tribal: The person holding the land is not a member of the protected tribal group.
predicates.statutory_land_status_unresolved: The character of the land or the nature of the interest transferred, which bears on statutory coverage, has not been resolved.

issues.definition: When a restoration proceeding concerns land whose statutory status is unresolved, the holder’s non-tribal status alone does not require reallocation to another tribal person.
